questions.question: Name the three tectonic forces, link each to its plate boundary, and explain the three conditions that decide whether stressed rock folds or faults.
questions.expected_answer: Compression drives rock together from opposite sides, shortening and thickening the crust, and operates at convergent boundaries. Tension pulls rock apart, stretching and thinning the crust, at divergent boundaries. Shearing drives adjacent rock in opposite directions along the same line at transform boundaries. Whether rock bends or breaks depends first on depth and temperature: deep rock is hot and confined by all-round pressure, so it deforms plastically and folds, while shallow rock is cold and brittle and fractures. Second, on the rate of stress: force applied slowly over millions of years lets rock creep into folds, while sudden force exceeds its strength and snaps it. Third, on rock type: thinly bedded sedimentary rocks such as shale and layered sandstone flex readily, while massive granite fractures. Under growing stress rock deforms elastically, then plastically past its elastic limit — folding — then fractures, and once the sides move the fracture is a fault.

questions.question: Using a labelled description rather than a drawing, explain the parts of a fold, the fold family in order of increasing compression, and how inversion of relief develops.
questions.expected_answer: In cross-section, an anticline is an upfold whose layers rise to a crest and dip away on both sides; a syncline is a downfold sagging to a trough. The tilted sides are limbs, shared between neighbouring folds; the line along the anticline's highest points is the axis, lying in the axial plane, and erosion exposes the oldest rock at an anticline's core because the deepest layers were lifted highest. With increasing compression the fold family runs: symmetrical, with limbs dipping equally; asymmetrical, leaning with one limb steeper; overfold, pushed past vertical so one limb overhangs; recumbent, lying flat on its side; and finally overthrust or nappe, where the rock shears along the axis and the upper limb is driven over the lower — the point where folding becomes faulting. Inversion of relief develops because the anticline's crest is stretched over the arch and full of cracks, so weathering and erosion attack it fastest, while the syncline's rock is squeezed dense; over time the arch may be excavated into a valley while the trough stands as a ridge, leaving the landscape upside down relative to its structure.

questions.question: Describe the formation and character of the Cape Fold Mountains, and show how their structure still shapes farming and roads in the Western Cape.
questions.expected_answer: The Cape Fold Mountains formed from the Cape Supergroup — sands and muds deposited in a shallow sea and hardened into extremely resistant quartzitic sandstone — which was buckled by compression from the south roughly 250 to 280 million years ago during the assembly of Gondwana. The result is the textbook fold-mountain pattern: long, narrow, parallel ranges separated by long, narrow valleys, in two trends — roughly north-south ranges such as the Olifants River Mountains and the Piketberg, and roughly west-east ranges such as the Riviersonderend, Kammanassie and Tsitsikamma — knotting together around Ceres. The sheltered valleys collect deep soils shed from the ridges and are watered by mountain rivers, so the Tulbagh basin grows deciduous fruit, the Robertson valley along the Breede grows wine grapes, and the coastal shelf below the Tsitsikamma carries forest and dairy. Because each range is a wall, roads cross only at passes such as Michell's Pass, the Tradouw Pass and Meiringspoort, and the region's road pattern still bends around the folds. As the mountains are old and no longer rising, erosion has locally inverted the relief, leaving some anticline cores as low ground while synclinal rock holds up the heights.
